R001.text: Let R=Z_(p), n=lambda+1, and e_i=y^i v/i! for 0<=i<=lambda. First prove these are a C-basis. Iterating [x,y]=h and [h,y]=-2y gives h(y^i v)=(lambda-2i)y^i v and, for 1<=i<=lambda, x(y^i v)=i(lambda-i+1)y^(i-1)v. Iterating the latter identity gives x^i y^i v=i! lambda(lambda-1)...(lambda-i+1)v. This scalar is nonzero in C and v is nonzero, so y^i v and e_i are nonzero (also e_0=v is nonzero). The h-eigenvalues alpha_i=lambda-2i are pairwise distinct: alpha_i-alpha_j=2(j-i) is nonzero in C for i!=j. For any relation sum_i c_i e_i=0, fix j and apply the operator product over k!=j of (h-alpha_k Id). Since h e_i=alpha_i e_i, this gives c_j product_{k!=j}(alpha_j-alpha_k)e_j=0, hence c_j=0; thus the e_i are linearly independent. There are lambda+1 of them and dim_C V(lambda)=lambda+1 by H004. If they did not span, adjoining a vector outside their span would give lambda+2 linearly independent vectors, contradicting that dimension. Thus they are a basis. Also y^(lambda+1)v, if nonzero, would be an h-eigenvector of eigenvalue -lambda-2 by the same h-y relation. This eigenvalue differs from every alpha_i, whereas in the established basis h is diagonal with eigenvalues alpha_0,...,alpha_lambda; a nonzero vector cannot be an eigenvector for another eigenvalue. Hence y^(lambda+1)v=0, and all higher y-powers vanish. The x-action stops at e_0 because xv=0, so higher x-powers on e_i vanish once their index would be negative. Iterating the relations therefore gives, for r>=0, X_r e_i=binom(lambda-i+r,r)e_(i-r) when 0<=r<=i and zero when r>i; and Y_r e_i=binom(i+r,r)e_(i+r) when i+r<=lambda and zero when i+r>lambda. In each case the zero is the just-proved termination of the respective string, not an assumption about an undefined basis vector. In the valid ranges these formulas follow by dividing x^r y^i v and y^(i+r)v by r!i! and using the displayed factorial coefficients. Thus the divided powers have integral matrices in this basis. Put M_R=R tensor_Z M inside V(lambda). Admissibility implies the R-algebra generated by all X_r,Y_r preserves M_R.

Using the basis proved in S001, define E_ab by E_ab(e_b)=e_a and E_ab(e_t)=0 for t!=b. The divided-power formulas give Y_lambda X_lambda=E_lambda,lambda: X_lambda kills e_i for i<lambda and sends e_lambda to e_0, while Y_lambda sends e_0 to e_lambda. They also give X_(lambda-i)E_lambda,lambda=E_i,lambda, since X_(lambda-i)e_lambda=e_i, and E_lambda,lambda Y_(lambda-j)=binom(lambda,j)E_lambda,j. Indeed, for an input e_k with k<j, the divided-power formula gives Y_(lambda-j)e_k=binom(k+lambda-j,lambda-j)e_(k+lambda-j), which is generally nonzero but has index less than lambda and is killed by E_lambda,lambda; for k=j it gives binom(lambda,j)e_lambda; and for k>j the Y-string has passed its endpoint, so Y_(lambda-j)e_k=0. Thus the stated identity is for the composite, not a claim that Y_(lambda-j) itself vanishes on every other basis vector. Since 0<=j<=lambda<p, neither lambda! nor j!(lambda-j)! is divisible by p, so binom(lambda,j) is a unit in R=Z_(p); this includes lambda=0 (the empty factorial is 1) and p=2. Therefore every E_i,j belongs to the R-algebra generated by the divided powers and preserves M_R.

For each i set J_i={c in C: c e_i is in M_R}. First, M_R is finite free over R: if m_1,...,m_n is the original Z-basis of M, then 1 tensor m_1,...,1 tensor m_n is an R-basis of R tensor_Z M, since the Z-coordinate isomorphism M≅Z^n extends to the explicit isomorphism R tensor_Z M≅R^n. The image E_i,i(M_R)=J_i e_i is finitely generated over R: it is the image of this finite module under the R-linear projection E_i,i. It is nonzero because M_R spans V(lambda) over C and E_i,i is a nonzero projection. Since E_i,j preserves M_R, applying it to c e_j proves J_j subset J_i; reversing i,j proves equality. Denote the common module by J. The coordinate projections give the internal direct sum M_R=⊕_{i=0}^{lambda} J e_i: each vector has its unique e-coordinate expansion, and its i-th coordinate belongs to J_i by the definition of J_i. Thus J is finitely generated (as just shown) and torsion-free, since it is an R-submodule of the field C and R is a domain. We now compute scalar-extension dimension before using any rank-one or ideal conclusion. Let Q=Frac(R), and let ι:Q tensor_R M_R→Q^n be the isomorphism obtained by extending the displayed original-basis coordinate isomorphism R tensor_Z M≅R^n; hence dim_Q(Q tensor_R M_R)=n. Tensor the coordinate direct-sum isomorphism with Q. The explicit compatible isomorphism ⊕_{i=0}^{lambda}(Q tensor_R J)→Q tensor_R M_R sends the i-th summand element q tensor c to q tensor(c e_i); its inverse is induced by the coordinate projections onto J e_i followed by e_i-coordinate extraction. Consequently, writing d=dim_Q(Q tensor_R J), finite because J is finitely generated, dimensions give n=(lambda+1)d=nd. Since n=lambda+1 is a positive integer, d=1. In particular the scalar-extension map μ:Q tensor_R J→C, q tensor c↦qc, is injective: Q tensor_R J is the localization of the R-submodule J⊂C, and an element maps to zero only if some nonzero denominator multiplier annihilates an element of J, which torsion-freeness forbids. Its image is nonzero (J is nonzero) and one-dimensional over Q, so choosing any nonzero image element identifies Q tensor_R J with Q as a Q-vector space. This proves the rank-one identification without assuming J free. Now use μ to regard J as a nonzero finitely generated R-submodule of Q. Clear denominators in a finite generating set to obtain a nonzero finitely generated ideal I of R with I=d_0J for some nonzero d_0 in R. Every nonzero q in Q is p^k u for an integer k and a unit u in R; among a finite set of nonzero generators of I choose the least exponent k. Every generator is in p^k R and one is p^k times a unit, so I=p^k R. Hence J is free of rank one. For a generator a of J, the vectors a e_i form an R-basis of M_R by the direct-sum decomposition.

For the generator a of J from F001, the vectors a e_i form an R-basis of M_R by the direct-sum decomposition and J=Ra proved in S003. Define b_i to be the image of a e_i in M_R/pM_R and then its image under (M_R/pM_R) tensor_F_p K = M tensor_Z K; these b_i form a K-basis. The divided-power formulas at r=1 give x(ae_i)=(lambda-i+1)ae_(i-1), y(ae_i)=(i+1)ae_(i+1), and h(ae_i)=(lambda-2i)ae_i, with the first term zero at i=0 (because xe_0=0) and the second zero at i=lambda (because y e_lambda=0 as established in S001). These integral action matrices reduce to exactly x b_i=(lambda-i+1)b_(i-1), y b_i=(i+1)b_(i+1), and h b_i=(lambda-2i)b_i over F_p and K, with the same endpoint zero actions. A Z-basis of M and its reduction identify M_R/pM_R with M tensor_Z F_p. Since K has characteristic p, extension of scalars identifies (M tensor_Z F_p) tensor_F_p K with M tensor_Z K and preserves these operator matrices. Thus this is an L(K)-module basis and action correspondence; no assumption that the h-eigenvalues remain distinct modulo p is involved.

For each 0<=r<=lambda<p, r! is invertible modulo p, so X_r and Y_r on the reduced module are the respective nonzero scalar multiples 1/r! of x^r and y^r; for r=0 the scalar is 1. The matrix-unit identities from S002 persist after reduction: their coefficients binom(lambda,j) are nonzero modulo p, and the same identities hold as operators on the K-basis b_0,...,b_lambda corresponding to the characteristic-zero e-basis. Thus any K-subspace W invariant under x and y is invariant under every E_i,j. Let W be arbitrary. If W=0, it is the zero subspace. For the other case, temporarily assume L1: W is nonzero. By the definition of nonzero subspace, there exists a vector w0 in W with w0 nonzero; record this existence before selecting w0 in S006.

By existential elimination applied to the existence fact F002, choose a witness w0 in W with w0 nonzero; its private identity is used only in this branch. Since b_0,...,b_lambda were established in S004 as a K-basis of M tensor_Z K, there are unique scalars c_i in K with w0=sum_i c_i b_i. At least one coefficient is nonzero, since if all c_i were zero the displayed expansion would give w0=0, contrary to the witness property. Choose an index i in the range 0<=i<=lambda with c_i nonzero; establish this existential fact before selecting i.

By existential elimination from F003 choose such an index i. For every j with 0<=j<=lambda, matrix-unit action gives E_j,i w0=c_i b_j. Because W is invariant under x and y it is invariant under E_j,i, so E_j,i w0 lies in W. The scalar c_i is nonzero in the field K and hence invertible; since W is a K-subspace, b_j=c_i^{-1}E_j,i w0 lies in W. This holds for each basis vector b_j, so W is the whole module. The chosen w0 and i are used only under L1.

The zero-subspace branch and the branch under L1 both establish that W is either zero or the whole module; discharge L1 by the two-case argument. The module has dimension lambda+1, which is positive because lambda>=0, so it is nonzero. Therefore it is irreducible as stated, including lambda=0 and p=2.
